answer: As requested, the original poster discovered the answer for himself: We're not sure [ 1 ][ 2 ]. We know that powered flight has evolved at least four times independently: Insects, Pterosaurs, Avians and Chiropterans [ 3 ][ 4 ][ 5 ][ 6 ]. However, with the stages that powered flight would have gone through to reach the modern state, it may be that various groups within each of these clades independently developed powered flight from other forms (gliding, leaping, etc) that was extremely similar to one another, and these other groups either went extinct or still collectively form a single clade, but powered flight is not a synapomorphy of the clade, and instead, all living members evolved in parallel [ 7 ][ 2 ]. The first link you mentioned does cover this specifically for bats, and the ideas are interesting, and very possible. The only problem with trying to confirm how powered flight evolved in these clades is that in order to become light enough for flight in general [ 11 ] (and before a species will begin optimising to be larger and capable of flight [ 4 ]), these animals often undergo extreme changes to their morphology, especially the shrinking and hollowing of their skeletons, which doesn't fossilize well [ 8 ], and thus makes these transition fossils special and difficult to find, most notably in the case of bats [ 9 ][ 10 ]. answer: Mating preference can be a genetic trait. That doesn't mean every sort of expressed preference (like the very wide range of human preferences, some of which are better ascribed to culture) is inherited, but in general we can expect that any behavior shared among a species must somehow be heritable, especially for species where cultural contributions can be ruled out (such as those in which the lifespans of generations do not overlap). The exact details are going to vary from species to species. Here are a couple examples... In this paper, the authors use artificial selection to show genetic transmission of a mating preference: The response to selection that we have demonstrated has taken place in the females' mating preference for quadrimaculata males. As shown in Table 3, when selected females are mated with males from the original stock, the level of preference is characteristic of the selected line; when selected males are mated with females from the original stock, the level of preference is characteristic of the original stock. Female mating preference has thus been shown to have a large genetic component in its determination. We believe that these experiments provide the first formal proof that a female mating strategy is genetically determined. Majerus, M. E. N., O'donald, P., & Weir, J. (1982). Female mating preference is genetic. Nature, 300(5892), 521-523. In this paper, the authors use an observational approach to show heritable variation within a population and use a pedigree approach to identify the inheritance pattern: Females of the arctiid moth Utetheisa ornatrix mate preferentially with larger males, receiving both direct phenotypic and indirect genetic benefits1. Here we demonstrate that the female's mating preference is inherited through the father rather than the mother, indicating that the preference gene or genes lie mostly or exclusively on the Z sex chromosome, which is strictly paternally inherited by daughters. Furthermore, we show that the preferred male trait and the female preference for that trait are correlated, as females with larger fathers have a stronger preference for larger males. Iyengar, V. answer: Yes . One test that I've done to determine the severity of my colourblindness is the Farnsworth D-15 . Basically you have to arrange a set of colours in order of gradual changes, and you can measure the severity of the colourblindness by how out-of-order they are. Note that doing an online version on a random website won't give you the best idea of the severity - my experience is that the random changes caused by eg night mode or just using a regular monitor screen make the test 'easier'. But you might have a different experience. When the results of trying to order the colours is shown in a circle, a person with normal vision will have a connected circle but the different severeties and types of colourblindness show different levels and directions of zig-zags. This website shows an example of a visual interpretation grading none-mild-severe but the wiki goes into some detail about attempts to quantify it. Here is a modified version of their image showing a severity gradation: The physical issue with colourblindness is that the eye lacks one (usually) of the three different types of colour receptor. answer: To clarify and close the question: Most papers on mathematical compost modeling assume that the compost mass remains constant, which I will refer to as the wet mass. This assumption is generally valid for an in-vessel compost reactor (a closed system), where moisture is assumed to remain contained within the system. The confusion may arise because some papers refer to the compost substrate $S$ , which is not the same as the wet mass. The substrate typically refers to the BVS (Biodegradable Volatile Solids), which decays over time, while the wet mass includes both the BVS and the inert or non-degradable mass, as well as moisture in the compost. When deriving the heat balance equation: $$\frac{d(cmT)}{dt} = \sum \dot{Q}$$ It logically follows that any heat generated from the BVS (Biodegradable Volatile Solids)—which represents the energy-producing portion of the compost—will be absorbed by the entire mass, including the wet mass. This accounts for the fact that heat energy is distributed across the total system, not just the decaying BVS fraction.

answer: I think you have your information a bit twisted here. Influenza virus in humans is still an airborne virus, the problem is that the virus doesn't transmit well between humans because of problems with the virus itself - usually the form of the hemagglutinin (HA) on the viral surface, which binds to sialic acids on the lung epithelium. In humans the sialic acids in the upper airway are predominantly α2,6-linked, while in the lower airway (i.e. deep in the lungs) they are predominantly α2,3-linked forms. Deep lung infections are difficult to transmit because it is hard to get the aerosols out of the lungs. So, virus forms with HA that bind α2,3-linked sialic acids won't transmit well between humans. It also means that viruses of this form can't easily infect humans as they generally need to get deep into the lung to do so. However, avian species, which are the majority of natural hosts for influenzas have it the other way around - they have α2,3-linked sialic acids at the surfaces where transmission is easiest. This is usually the gut in birds, rather than the lungs, but the mechanism of viral attachment and aerosol spread hold true for both birds and humans. So, there is a barrier between humans and avian species in terms of viruses they put out and how they infect. This isn't to say that influenzas that bind best to α2,3-linked sialic acids won't infect humans at all, they certainly can do so and will given the opportunity, but they generate an infection that doesn't transmit well human-to-human. Rob Mettelman and Paul Thomas wrote a freely available review of influenza infectivity in humans titled " Human Susceptibility to Influenza Infection and Severe Disease " 1 , if you need more information. Ref: Mettelman RC, Thomas PG. Human Susceptibility to Influenza Infection and Severe Disease. Cold Spring Harb Perspect Med. 2021 May 3;11(5):a038711. doi: 10.1101/cshperspect.a038711. PMID: 31964647; PMCID: PMC8091954.

answer: To test for phages plate a 10-fold dilution series from 10 -1 to 10 -10 in soft agar overlays (0.75% agar in your broth of choice) with 100 ul of overnight bacterial culture and at some point(s) you should get clear countable plaques. This methodology has been around for a long time, since at least Gratia in 1936 1 and is very easy. Phages should also be filterable with a 0.1 um filter, but you'd need so much plasmid volume that it probably isn't worth it, though you could dilute the plasmid in buffer, filter, and then concentrate the DNA again. DNA extraction followed by gel separation is likely to be your best route. Any extraction protocol that contains either phenol (e.g. plain phenol-chloroform extraction) and/or guanidinium chloride (e.g. Trizol) should work well. This will extract both phage and plasmid DNA! As the above will also extract the phage DNA (assuming it is a DNA phage). When you transform the bacteria from this prep, the phage will be generated from its DNA. So, you need to separate the phage DNA from the plasmid. Generally, the easiest way to do this will be by size separation followed by gel-extraction. Simply run the DNA on a gel and perform a gel extraction on an appropriate sized band. You might want to consider digesting the plasmid with a single-site restriction endonuclease and re-circularizing after the extraction so as to allow you to get all your plasmid in a single band rather than spread across the various forms that plasmids can make, such as supercoiled, nicked and linear. You do need quite a bit of DNA to get a decent gel extraction; the returns are often less than 10% of input, but you only need a tiny amount to transform bacteria. Something in the nanogram range can work just fine for transformation. The caveat to the above is that your plasmid and the phage genome might be around the same size, so separation of the two on a gel could be difficult. In that case, you are likely to be best off simply amplifying your insert by PCR and ligating it into a new empty backbone. This is a simple process and generally very quick if your insert isn't enormous (>3000 bp) or you if you don't have some special needs with specific frame insertion requirements, or anything else which requires a bit of thought to perform. You can also amplify the backbone and use that too, but bigger PCRs can be difficult and cause errors in critical regions within the plasmid. A third option, if you knew which phage it was and had the genome, is that you could potentially choose a few restriction endonucleases that would digest the phage DNA but not the plasmid. Use 1-2 of those on your plasmid prep and re-transform. You'd want to be sure that your digest was successful, so doing a phage assay on the resulting culture would be essential. You could also potentially size separate and gel extract after the digest to remove any undigested phage DNA. If phages are present in your stock of competent bacteria, you are out of luck; you'll be best to get more bacteria from a clean source. You can either do this commercially through a company, or from a colleague, or from a cell bank. Apparently there are antibiotics that can inhibit phage infection, but I don't know how effective they will be, and most of the indicated substances will kill E. coli . See table 4 in this paper from Karczewska et al. 2023 2 . Phages easily contaminate equipment, so be sure to give your pipettes a thorough clean inside the barrel and on the tip ejector. 0.25% hypochlorite (made from bleach) will do nicely. Otherwise autoclave them if you can. Quaternary ammonium compounds can work too, but you need to meet the exposure times and they are not as effective. Reference: Gratia A. Numerical Relationships between Lysogenic Bacteria and Particles of Bacteriophage. Ann Inst Pasteur. 1936;57:652. Karczewska M, Strzelecki P, Szalewska-Pałasz A, Nowicki D. How to Tackle Bacteriophages: The Review of Approaches with Mechanistic Insight. Int J Mol Sci. 2023 Feb 23;24(5):4447. doi: 10.3390/ijms24054447. PMID: 36901878; PMCID: PMC10003480.

answer: I've not read the press release, but I can tell you unequivocally that these are not dire wolves ( Aenocyon dirus ). These are grey wolves tweaked for some characteristics. Simply put, they have taken a grey wolf ( Canis lupus lupus ) and tweaked some genes, I think around 20ish genes from the media stories I have seen. These genes are particularly those that make the head larger and muscles stronger. These alter the external appearance of the wolf to look more like dire wolves. Grey wolves and dire wolves, as you can see from the scientific names, are from separate genera within the dog ( Canidae ) family. This means that, while they are related, there is a distant genetic relationship. You could think of this as being similar to the relationship between humans (genus Homo ) and chimpanzees (genus Pan ). The genomes of humans and chimpanzees are very similar, at around 98-99% similarity. However, tweaking a few genes of a human to make them shorter, with longer, coarser hair, longer arms, different pelvis shape and greater strength does not make them a chimpanzee. By the same logic tweaking some genes in a wolf does not make it a dire wolf. In addition, while dire wolves and wolves co-existed recently, we really only have sub-fossil remains with ancient DNA in them. This means fragmented DNA which is hard to extract and is very difficult to work with. The technology to work with ancient DNA is amazing and advancing rapidly, but the very nature of it means working with partial samples and a lot of reconstruction bioinformatically. Further supporting my point, a 2021 study from Perri et al. 1 found that the genomes of dire wolves and grey wolves were highly divergent, and that dire wolves were the last of an ancient divergent lineage of canids, with little genetic relatedness to members of the Canis genus, and that there is no evidence of gene flow between the two genera. A third complication is that, while we have the genomes and could potentially tweak genes to suit, a whole lot of what goes into making a species a species is all the bits of the genome that aren't encoded in the genes. Only a few years ago, these bits of the genome were called "junk DNA", and were thought to not do much, but recent evidence is that they do plenty. There are all sorts of gene regulations that go on in these regions (promoters, epigenetic modifications and many more) and it all alters how genes behave and hence how the animal looks, behaves and many other factors. Currently, we don't know a huge amount how these regions of the genome work, even for such well studied organisms as mice, but people are working on it. This lack of knowledge means that we can't currently make anything that we can actually call a dire wolf, merely something that looks like one. So, to answer your questions in your second to last paragraph - they are the species that was modified - grey wolf, they are not a new species at all. They are very close to grey wolves genetically, with modifications to only a handful of genes, whereas the dire wolf was quite genetically distinct from the grey wolf it would seem. I could see an argument for these being hybrids, but I would say most hybrids have more genetic mixing going on than we see here. Perhaps "variant" might be a better description, but even that might be too strong a word. answer: Gigantism in baleen whales is a trait that developed very recently in their evolutionary history, within the last 3 million years [ 1 ]. Before that time period, many species of these whales rarely exceeded 10 metres. The size of a whale appears to be historically related to how big the bait balls of their prey get, and the amount of baleen they need to filter large quantities [ 2 ]. The informally named Plio-Pleistocene period changed the dynamics of ocean ecosystems, one of the side effects of which was the frequent formation of high-prey-density zones [ 3 ]. Their feeding strategy (ramming & gulping) is significantly related to the impact of size on their fitness, and an increase in size developed multiple times independently in many whale species [ 4 ][ 5 ]. It is important to also understand that baleen whales are active animals and descended from active predators, so a slow, almost sessile filter-feeding strategy has a longer evolutionary path to stability than the gulping and ramming strategy, and were thus out-competed [ 2 ][ 6 ]. Also, baleen whales largely consume krill (especially the blue whale, which exclusively eats krill) and small filter-feeding fish largely consume plankton and nutrient particles [ 7 ], so a diet difference does have an apparent influence on size. TLDR: Baleen whales feed by ramming and gulping, which requires being large enough to consume bait balls in droves. This strategy is evolutionarily stable and has seen no trends today towards filter-feedings strategies used by smaller organisms such as krill and forage fish. In fact, there is evidence that multiple baleen whale species are being sexually selected to be even larger, particularly the blue whale [ 8 ][ 9 ].

answer: Often in popular explanations, we hear that organisms evolved these features "because they needed them" for survival. Ya, that's very, very wrong. Evolution is a stochastic or chance process. According to Hugo de Vries theory of evolution , evolution occurs due to random sudden huge mutations that occur in any random direction. So evolution is not at all a directed process. When these variations occur, they could either benefit the organism or harm it. In case of useful variations, the organisms have a benefit over other organisms of its type. For example, if there are a group of herbivores without eyes, and one of them suddenly develops eyes, it would surely have a benefit because it can see where vegetation is to feed upon. (Point to note here is that this is just an example, and evolution of the eye has been described below) This in Darwin's terms, is often known as "Survival of the fittest". So, "need" has no role in this process. "Environmental pressure" does have a role in this, especially for selecting the better traits. For example, in Lederberg's replica plating experiment , bacteria which had pre-evolved antibiotic resistance survived due to the selection pressure of the antibiotic environment. Darwin's theory and Neo Darwinism Neo-Darwinism is the most recent theory of evolution. Let us discuss Darwin's theory first: Important role of reproduction: Organisms reproducing at a very high rate make more of themselves, and out compete others. Struggle for existence: This high rate of reproduction leads to competition for food, land, etc. Variation and their Inheritance: Organism have inbuilt variation for providing benefits to the organism. Survival of the fittest and natural selection: Organisms with the best of these characteristics succeed in this competition and produce more organisms with its beneficial characteristics. In this case, variations originate randomly. The organism with better characteristics has a reproductive advantage, therefore increasing the number of individuals having that characteristic in the population. Better characteristics get selected and genetically passed on. When the Mendelian genetics are added on this theory, it is known as Neo-Darwinism. In this theory as well, new genes are produced through random mutations. Slow variations over time accumulate to give new characters like eyes. This theory differs from the de Vries theory, as it says that slow variations keep on accumulating rather than a single large variation. This theory is more applicable to your example of the eye, as it evolved slowly from "photospots" to more complex forms like ommatidia and the eyes in case of vertebrates, instead of a sudden huge mutation. This has been described below. An insight into the evolution of the eye Short look into the rapid evolution of the eye: The eye began not as a tool for “seeing” but as a simple light detector, first appearing as photospots or ocelli in euglenoids to gauge light for photosynthesis. Primitive light-sensing structures, such as pigment spot ocelli found in jellyfish, flatworms, and even alongside compound eyes in insects, represent early stages in this journey. In vertebrates, fossil evidence indicates eyes emerged with the first fish during the Cambrian period, with their structure remaining largely unchanged for over 400 million years, as seen in modern lampreys. Nilsson and Pelger’s 1994 modeling suggested that a complex fish-type eye could evolve surprisingly quickly—within half a million years—from a light-sensitive patch of skin. Evolution has repeatedly produced eyes through convergence, leading to striking similarities like those between fish and cephalopods. Biochemically, this innovation rested on opsin proteins, derived from ancestral GPCRs, which bound retinal to enable light sensitivity. While alternative light-absorbing molecules existed, rhodopsins and cryptochromes outcompeted them, forming the foundation for animal vision. Image of evolution of the eye in Mollusca Nereis virens —King sandworm: note the eyecup but no lens. This provides some spatial information for the animal although its vision is poor. Nevertheless, it is a predator. Histologic section by Richard Dubielzig DVM. Nautilus: note the nautilus eye with a pinhole but no cornea. The eye is embedded with the body with the histology seen in. A much, much more detailed one : The eye originally evolved as something we don't think of it as "eyes" today. It evolved the sensation of light (the ability to detect light) in its surrounding rather than "looking at and scanning" it's surroundings. "Photospot" or "stigma" originally evolved in the euglenoids for helping in detection of light intensity for photosynthesis. It contains the chemical astaxanthin. The halophiles (primitive archaea) develop a pigmented membrane composed of a pigment called bacterio-rhodopsin (related to the one found in our own eyes) to harness the sun's energy. The light energy is utilised to carry on ATP production but they cannot use this ATP in food synthesis. Hence, they are heterotrophs. Bacteriorhodopsin is defined as a light-driven ion pump found in the purple membrane of Halobacterium salinarum , consisting of trimers of monomers that contain seven transmembrane $\alpha$ -helices and a retinal molecule, facilitating proton pumping through a photochemical cycle linked to retinal photoisomerization and protein conformational changes. Ocellus ("simple eye or photospot") is a quite primitive form of the eye, although it might not be as simple as the name suggests. Some organisms like some jellyfish, sea stars, flatworms, and ribbonworms may have primitive light sensors as the only means of "seeing". These light sensing cells are called pigment spot ocelli , which have randomly distributed pigment, and have no other higher structures such as a cornea or lens). In arthropods like cockroaches and wasps, these might be present addition to the complex eye. Head of Polistes with two compound eyes and three ocelli (circled) In the animal kingdom, it evolved in a similar manner (see pictures above for details). Fish fossils from these periods have eye sockets, indicating that these fish must have had eyes. The lampreys, present-day relatives of these early fish, have eyes that are very similar to those of other fish, leading to the conclusion that very little has happened to the aquatic form of the vertebrate eye for about 400 million years. The lower chordates, from which the vertebrates arose, have either simple eyespots or no eyes at all; therefore, presumably the vertebrate eye originated with the first fish and not before. Discussing about the time required for this evolutionary success I found out this 1994 experiment, In 1994 Swedish zoologists Dan-Eric Nilsson and Susanne Pelger took up the challenge of “evolving” an eye of the fish type from a patch of photosensitive skin. Using pessimistic estimates of variation, heritability, and selection intensity, Nilsson and Pelger came to the conclusion that it would take 364,000 generations for a fish eye to evolve. Given a generation time of a year, which is typical for moderate-sized animals, a respectable eye could evolve in less than half a million years. Of course, other physiological elements (e.g., competent brains) have to evolve in parallel with eyes. However, at least as far as the eye itself is concerned, very little time is actually required for its evolution. This evolution mostly occurred in the Cambrian period, with small changes occurring outside of it. Evolution of the eye has occurred several times. Because there are only a limited number of ways that images can be produced, it is not surprising that some of them have been “discovered” more than once. This has led to numerous examples of convergence in the evolutionary history of eyes. The similarity in optical design of the eyes of fish and cephalopod molluscs, such as octopuses and squid, is perhaps the most well-known example. Biochemical aspect: (from The evolution of eyes: major steps. The Keeler lecture 2017 ) The opsin in rhodopsin probably evolved from a G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR) protein although this origin is murky. G proteins are rather common and rather easily produced, but the first ‘opsins’ were not true GPCR. Rather these early opsin-like compounds combined with retinal that functioned as a proton pump for energy production for certain Archaea. The passage of such molecules from microbial opsins to metazoan opsins probably came from a common ancestor as these are related, albeit distantly. Retinal and its eventual congeners and an opsin served as the basis for the principal family of metazoan photoreceptive compounds—the ciliary opsins, rhabdomeric opsins, and the photoisomerases. These were not the only photoreceptive compounds available to first life as other compounds such as the flavins, porphyrins, biliproteins, and chlorophyll among others could have been sufficient for the transduction of light to the energy to power a biochemical signal. However, under certain circumstances these compounds could be toxic or photosensitizing to cells. These other compounds were not able to compete as successfully with rhodopsin for the principal photoreceptive one although the flavins are retained in many Metazoa as light-sensing molecules in the form of cryptochromes. This biochemistry was crucial to our use of rhodopsin and cryptochromes. Two other questions that are good to read in the context of the evolution of the eye: What is the minimum eye? An example would be Kimberella (described here) which might or might not have been a mollusc and might or might not have had photoreceptors! So, this is the first time it evolved in Animalia. answer: The phenomenon you're interested in is called abscission, and in the case of falling leaves occurs along a well-defined layer of cells at the base of the leaf. To briefly summarize wikipedia: following a period of nutrient resorption, the plant will engage mechanisms to create a protective layer and detach the leaf. The protective layer usually includes production of lignin and suberin, polymers that are both durable and waterproof. The detachment can occur by different mechanisms, but commonly involves enzymatic degradation of the middle lamella, which is a layer between cells that cements them together. Another mechanism is imbibition, where cells in the abscission layer take in so much water that they burst, causing a break along the layer. answer: I think this sort of question is better answered by thought experiment and theory than by empirical study because of all the potential variability in defining "indoor space" and since the underlying principles are pretty simple and direct. Animals like humans produce CO 2 by 'burning' biomass . Plants sequester CO 2 by producing biomass. There's no other magic place that CO 2 goes: the net is from biomass produced. Therefore, to offset the CO 2 for one human sitting around producing it, you'd need an indoor plant to produce as much biomass as a human eats in a day. For just oxygen concerns it wouldn't have to be actually edible/digestible biomass, but that still provides a rough imagination. There are a variety of estimates for how much total land that would take, see e.g.: https://gardening.stackexchange.com/questions/1433/how-large-a-cultivation-area-to-feed-one-person but all of these estimates are quite a bit more than the space typically committed to house plants in the space that a human occupies. You can also look at attempts at indoor closed ecosystems, like Biosphere 2 ; these used quite a bit more space (acres) and far more plant material than a typical houseplant contributes. The issue has also been looked at for space exploration purposes. Some existing SE Q&A at Space.SE have some useful calculations, e.g.: https://space.stackexchange.com/questions/26668/how-many-plants-would-be-needed-to-produce-oxygen-enough-for-20-humans From one answer, https://space.stackexchange.com/a/26711/25058 The quick summary is about 300 to 500 typical domestic houseplants per person, with significant caveats, more like 700 to be safe. So 6-14 thousand such plants for 20 people. We see below that our 20 humans need 17kg of oxygen per day between them, which is more or less 1000 mol. This means the plants need to add 160 mol of glucose to their dry mass, which is about 30kg. So you need enough plants to produce 30kg dry mass of new plant per day. Overall, my answer to the title question would be "No.", with the caveat that of course an arbitrarily large number of plants, more than a typical indoor space would have, could theoretically do so. But, from a practical engineering sense, assuming you're on Earth you'd be better off exchanging with outside air that plants from a much bigger area than your indoor space have already conditioned with reduced CO 2 .

answer: Pistachios in the shops are dried fruit, the outer hull (sometimes referred to as pericarp, sometimes exocarp) being relatively opaque. The kernels of pistachio nuts (technically seeds in the botanical sense, but "nuts" for culinary purposes) produce chlorophyll from early in development even before they are sufficiently mature to grow independently. The earlier they are harvested, the more green they tend to be as they lose the vivid colour as they mature, turning a brown colour as the green fades from parts of the surface of the cotyledon. The greenness varies quite a bit by variety and irrigation; Sicily, Italy and Turkey producing the greenest varieties particularly when well hydrated during growth. The light exposure of the plant during critical growth phases markedly affects the colour of the fruit. Wild pistachios: At first glance it may be imagined that the green colour is present in un-ripened fruit as a result of selective breeding perhaps as a marketable and valuable trait that was selected for, but the wild relatives (P. vera, P. atlantica, P. khinjuk etc.) exhibit a similar pattern of colour development and fading. Some of the wild varieties seem to exhibit even deeper colouration than their cultivated counterparts, some are paler or more brown/black. The persistence of the colour green is apparently increased by the plant being in partial shade during final maturation. Chlorophylls during development: Tomato seeds are known to develop high levels of chlorophylls during embryogenesis which fade later as the fruit matures. These are thought to aid in formation of seed-oils and then as the seeds mature, the process slows and stops to prevent the build-up of reactive oxygen species that can damage the embryo. In pistachios, phenolic compounds, terpenes and flavonoids within the seed act to counteract this damage to some degree allowing latitude for photosynthesis to continue further into seed development. The partial transparency of the growing fruit allows some light through, the hull losing its green colour and becoming more opaque as it dries, often dehiscing (splitting) when ripe. The colour change is a signal to growers that the harvest time is upon them, but timing of harvest varies according to business practices, practical considerations and perhaps some preference of a greener fruit (citation needed). Conclusion: The hull is translucent-green and fruit is green and photosynthetic during development enabling laying down of essential energy storage and contributing towards growth, this fades on maturation as the hull becomes opaque and dries - this helps prevent oxidative damage during the latter stages. The chlorophyll is produced again on germination for growth. answer: Mimicry such as the kind you’ve found is not unusual in nature, especially in insects that are heavily preyed upon. Examples even more striking (imo) exist, including the Middle Eastern fruit fly Goniurellia tridens, which also has insect-like markings on its wings. This particular marking may confuse predators or may resemble an undesirable prey insect (e.g. an ant or spider) upon which the predator does not feed. Like your own example, this insect initially had a small mark that somehow provided a survival advantage, thereby also giving it an advantage over others to mate and pass on the mark. Every time the mark changed a bit through mutation, the individual carrying the advantageous mark (as opposed to a disadvantageous or neutral mark) had a survival advantage it could pass on, until its progeny has become what you see today (and in which mutations are still occurring.) There is no example of the spontaneous development of such an intricate advantageous marking that I aware of. Tremendous survival advantages can occur with one mutation, but these tend to be in the changed expression of a gene (e.g. the continued expression of lactase beyond infancy in humans.) Mimicry evolves over generations of selection. See mimicry in Wikipedia.

answer: Paying the statement balance each month is not the same as 0% utilization. 0% utilization means that you didn't use the card at all that month, or you made payments to get the balance to zero before the monthly statement was created. The balance that gets reported to the credit bureaus is typically the statement balance on your card, not the balance after you make a payment. The "utilization" that the credit scorers calculate is therefore based on how much you put on the card over the month, not how much you float from month to month. The reason to pay at least the statement balance every month is not to build credit, but to avoid paying interest . You get the same benefit to your credit score by making a minimum payment on time, but you'll get charged 2% interest (24% annualized) or more on the remaining balance each month. (It's actually charged on more than the remaining balance, but that's not the point here) For example, if your credit limit is $10,000 and you want to have a 6% utilization (I'm not saying that's the perfect amount, just an example) then you would try to spend about $600 each month and pay it off each month . I would also note that your payment history is generally a bigger factor than utilization. Utilization is more to measure if you're using too much credit, or have too much to use (meaning you could theoretically go on a shopping spree). If you pay your bills each month and don't use too much credit you'll be fine. Secondly, your credit score is not a measure of how good you are with money. It's a measure of how likely you are to pay off your debts . There is very little benefit to making it "as high as possible" other than personal feelings. My credit score has wavered between 750 and 820 and the variance has had absolutely no impact on my ability to get loans or any other aspect of my life. There are negative consequences for low credit scores if you want to borrow money, but those are because of bad behavior that make you a possible credit risk (trust is hard to earn but easy to lose). The only thing a max credit score gets you is a little more grace if you mess up once. What is the correct percent of utilization to keep on your credit cards for the best possible credit score? Is it zero, or non-zero (one percent, two percent, anything below six percent)? It's not zero but no one knows the exact percentage. It may also be the case where the "best" percentage is different depending on other factors.

answer: "Risk" is a word that has many different meanings, especially in Finance. It's important to understand what type of risk (or more specifically, risk of what) you're trying to understand. In a diversification context, there are two types of risk that are involved. One common use of "risk" is "variance of returns". In a portfolio, the variance of returns depends not only on the variance of individual securities, but also how that are correlated. If two securities are perfectly correlated, then their total variance will just be the sum of the individual variances (I'm simplifying the math a bit here). If two securities are uncorrelated, or less than perfectly correlated, their total variance will be less than the sum. If they are perfectly negatively correlated (as one moves up, the other moves down an equal amount), then the total variance will be zero. So diversification , or choosing investments that are at worst loosely correlated, will reduce the variance of returns. As some stocks go up, others will go down, reducing the variance. It's also used to distinguish between idiosyncratic (or "unsystematic") risk and systemic risk as you mention. The market itself has some inherent risk that you can't diversify away, but you can reduce variance by investing in multiple loosely correlated markets, which reduces variance just like diversifying stocks. To answer your question, it can eliminate some types of risk and can reduce overall risk, but it cannot eliminate risk altogether. But there are other types of risk that you and others mention - risk can also means "probability of something bad happening" like a market crash, or an asteroid. That type of risk can't be mitigated by diversification, but rather through other means like stop losses.

answer: If the organization is going under, as an independent contractor, you're in the back of the line with all the other unsecured creditors. answer: The credit card companies are required by network rules to refund transactions where the purchased product/service was not in fact supplied. They then charge that back to the merchant. answer: You're intentionally investing in stocks that you hope will lose value, so you'll have losses you can realize in order to offset the gains in the index fund. This is not a sound investing strategy -- since capital gains tax is only around 10-15%, depending on your tax bracket, the losses you incur will be much more than the tax savings. As someone commented, this is what is called "letting the tax tail wag the investing dog". You're buying losers just so you can reduce your taxes, even though it means your net after-tax returns will be lower. This is fine if your goal is to "stick it" to the government, but not if you're trying to save money yourself. In addition, it's not likely to make that much of a dent in the gains you'll get from selling the index fund. If you've been invested there for many years, your unrealized gains will be sizeable. Meanwhile, you'll only be invested in these individual stocks for a couple of years, so they won't have had a chance to drop much. You're going to invest a small amount in each of a handful of stocks -- even if it drops 10%, that's 10% of a small amount. answer: Any two people who are close enough to call for help in a distressing situation should ideally set up a code word, a code phrase or a challenge / response in advance. It’s easy and it’s practically impossible to hack as long as you don’t ever share this information with anyone else or type it out anywhere . Example: If I say "Annapolis" to my sister, she has to answer, "watermelon". It makes no sense to anyone but us, and that's perfect. For people who don’t have the foresight to prepare in advance, you need to tell the caller that you have to verify their identity to make sure it’s not a scam, then ask them a question or two that is probably not written anywhere in print or online, or which occurred before the internet era. If they become defensive and “just can’t believe you would make them go through this in an emergency”, hang up – it’s a scammer. Then take a breath, think for a moment, and ask questions that only the caller or someone else in your inner circle would know. A few random examples: Q: What instrument did Mom’s father play? answer: The trick is this: Car dealerships often make money off the loans they provide to customers, as well as the sales of actual cars. Loan companies pay the car dealerships a commission when a customer of the dealer takes a loan out with the loan company. Most car salesmen are therefore incentivized to sell clients loans, in the same way that they are incentivized to sell cars. Put simply, they get extra commission when you take out a loan. The dealership itself is also probably rewarded. Therefore they are happy to cut a bit off the price of the car in order to get you to do it (and especially happy to give you a rebate, which doesn't reduce the actual price of the car and thus means you don't take a smaller loan.) Neither of them care what happens to the loan once it is taken out. They already have their money. If everything is as they say it is, this "trick" doesn't hurt you at all. You get a cheaper car, they get their money for selling you a loan, and you get to pay off the loan immediately. Only the loan company loses, and they are playing the odds to they don't really care either. Of course the problem is when things don't work out exactly like the salesman says. For example there may be fees associated with paying back the loan, or it may take a couple of months before you can do it, or some kind of assumed interest even when you've paid it back, or something. You should make sure you completely understand what would happen, that you've read and understood the terms of the loan, and you get something in writing signed by the salesman saying how you do this. Also get a quote for what it would cost if you paid cash so you can compare.

answer: See Section 5(4) of the Theft Act of 1968, which clearly applies to this situation in the UK. Where a person gets property by another’s mistake, and is under an obligation to make restoration (in whole or in part) of the property or its proceeds or of the value thereof, then to the extent of that obligation the property or proceeds shall be regarded (as against him) as belonging to the person entitled to restoration, and an intention not to make restoration shall be regarded accordingly as an intention to deprive that person of the property or proceeds. Knowingly retaining funds that have been accidentally deposited to your account, after being so informed, is a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison. Spending those funds is the additional crime of theft. So take the high road! To be sure it's not a scam of some kind, verify the identity of those claiming that the payment was made in error, and then return the funds forthwith. ADDENDUM To address the quibbling in comments regarding the phrase "and is under an obligation to make restoration", this wording in the Act is likely intended to avoid criminalizing ordinary business disputes over what constitutes a mistaken payment. UK law allows very limited exceptions to the obligation. For example -- Company "A" issues an invoice to company "B" with terms Net 30. B has cash flow problems and intends to pay after 90 days in an attempt to forestall insolvency, but a clerk at company B mistakenly pays it in 30 days. Financial chaos ensues at company B, who want the payment returned. Under UK law, A is under no obligation to return the funds that were mistakenly paid , and the Act does not apply.

answer: CO2, O3, and CH4, which constitute, in combination, approximately only 0.04% of the atmosphere's mass A minor nitpick here: these gases constitute about 0.04% of the atmosphere by mole fraction , i.e. number of molecules. Since a molecule of CO2 is heavier than a molecule of O2 or N2, the percentage by mass would be a bit higher than this. Although these gases only make up approx. 0.04% of the atmosphere, there is quite a lot of atmosphere, so 0.04% is still quite a lot. Consider a photon travelling through the atmosphere in a straight line. How long before it collides with a molecule in the air? The average distance between such collisions is called the " mean free path ". At sea level, the MFP is about 65 nanometres; to put it another way, for every metre our photon travels, it will collide with approximately fifteen million air molecules. [Air also contains argon, which is found as individual atoms rather than molecules, but for brevity let's take "molecules" to mean "molecules and/or argon atoms" here.] Calling these "collisions" is a bit misleading, because most of these interactions are pretty inconsequential. When the photon meets an oxygen or nitrogen molecule, or an argon atom, it's likely to just keep going, barely affected by that interaction. But about 0.4% of the molecules it might encounter are H2O, and 0.04% are CO2 or other GHGs.* That means that for every meter our photon travels, it will interact with approximately sixty thousand water molecules and six thousand CO2/other GHG molecules. For a heat-carrying photon to escape into space from the surface of the Earth, it has to make it through many millions of such interactions. Even if each interaction has only a small chance of capturing that photon, those tiny chances add up when there are so many of them. (And meanwhile it also has billions of interactions with O2/N2/Ar, but those are less likely to capture it.) *This ignores the fact that different molecules have different sizes and larger molecules are more likely to get hit. If we were trying to do an exact calculation we'd want to take that into account, but that's not the level we're working at here.

question: How do seasonal changes affect tides/sea level?
question_context: I'm currently doing the theoretical part of an advanced sailing certificate, which involves tidal calculations using the admiralty tide tables (ATT). In these, the times and heights of every high and low water in the given year are tabulated for a few ports called standard ports. For other ports called secondary ports, there are adjustment offsets with which you can calculate time and height at the secondary port if you have them for its corresponding standard port. One of these adjustments are "seasonal changes in mean level" (quote from the ATT), which are offsets to the water level based on the month. E.g., on January 1st 2005, the water level in Nantes in 0.1m higher than in its standard port Brest, on July 1st it is 0.3m lower (the exercise material contains an excerpt of the ATTs from 2005). The way these adjustments are applied in the standardized prediction form is by finding time and height of the relevant high and low water at the standard port, subtracting the seasonal changes at the standard port (since they're already integrated into the tabulated data and need to be neutralized), applying the main adjustment offset, and finally adding the seasonal changes at the secondary port. The explanation I've been given for these seasonal changes is that the tidal force changes with earth's distance from the sun. At perihelion (early January) it's stronger, at aphelion (early July) it's weaker. What I don't understand about this is that the adjustment is applied with the same sign to both high and low water. But if was about the strength of the tidal force, I'd just expect more "springy" springs and less "neapy" neaps at perihelion, and conversely less "springy" springs and more "neapy" neaps at aphelion. I'd expect that I have to apply the seasonal correction with different sign for high and low water, because the tidal range grows or shrinks from both ends. Applying them with the same sign implies that the mean sea level changes over the year, and that this change differs between nearby locations. The explanation is also offered on a NOAA website which states (emphasis mine): When the Earth is closest to the sun (perihelion), around January 2 of the calendar year, tidal ranges are enhanced . At aphelion, when the Earth is furthest from the sun, around July 2, tidal ranges are reduced . The seasonal change data I have available tends to have slightly positive values around January, and slightly negative values around July (it's not very consistent though, and in some cases it doesn't match). So the explanation would actually make a little sense if you add the offset for high water, but subtract it for low water. Another website claims that water levels can change seasonally with prevailing weather patterns or temperature and density of the water: Seasonally, water levels can also change depending especially on changes in the prevailing wind direction, and meteorological phenomena - some of which were discussed above, but might also include changes in seasonal runoff, climate oscillations (i.e., El Nino, etc.), and even seasonal changes in the temperature and density of water. This makes more sense as a reason for treating high and low water with the same sign. Yet another website states that contraction and expansion due to water temperature is a major factor, but also weather patterns and ocean currents: An important cause of intra-annual sea level change is the annual warming/cooling cycle – in each hemisphere the oceans warm and expand in summer, and cool and contract in the winter. Thus the sea levels in each hemisphere are higher in summer and early autumn, and lower in winter and early spring. In a convective rainfall setting during summer, if your thunderstorm cell misses your station by 1 km, is it still a bad forecast? answer: It resembles case hardening to me. This process is described in the Wikipedia article https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Case_hardening_of_rocks and in several papers. It is unlikely to be desiccation cracks, because the pattern appears to wrap around the boulder rather than follow planar surfaces. If case hardening is the cause, the texture should encircle the outer surface of the rock but should not extend deeply into the interior, as it typically develops only within the outer millimeters to a few centimeters after prolonged exposure. The texture forms when the outermost layer of the rock becomes chemically hardened during weathering. Near the surface, water can precipitate iron, manganese, or silica, producing a cemented crust that is mechanically stronger than the underlying material. As stresses accumulate through expansion–contraction cycles and moisture changes, this rigid shell begins to fracture into polygonal plates. Subsequent erosion accentuates those boundaries and creates the characteristic scaly appearance. The phenomenon develops slowly and does not occur while the rock is still part of fresh bedrock. Case hardening is especially common in sandstone because its porosity allows water to circulate through the rock, dissolve cement from the interior, and re-precipitate it near the surface where water evaporates. This process gradually creates a thin outer shell that is far more strongly cemented than the underlying material.

answer: Rock is defined as solid material which is not ice or other volatile materials like CO or CO2. That implies that anything ionized cannot be considered rock any longer - and the border to "being rock" is IMHO already above that. Of course you can break down any matter into its constituents in a heavy ion collider like LHC at CERN - but matter would have lost its relation to "rockiness" at the stage it got ionized and either molten, evaporated and/or ionized. The smallest solid particles as formed from condensation of the gas phase in the creation of solar systems are typically starting at a few nanometers in diameter, thus a few hundred atoms in size. Yet even when it is solid material at that stage, usually a rock is something bigger than a fine-grained material which exhibits bulk properties other than a large chunk of the same material. Thus rockiness usually starts to be referred to from sizes you can start to handle individually with your fingers, maybe cm or a few cm. Generally the relation of the size of your 'rock' in relation to the total system size you consider is important for assessment of the physical properties of the system you want to look at (granular vs. solid).

answer: "Shaking" is the normal way excess energy is dissipated in solids Earthquakes usually occur when there is a sudden release of stress caused when blocks of crustal rocks move. Often this is because two blocks are on different moving plates but are normally "stuck" until the stress is large enough to cause slippage of to break the integrity of the rock. Some earthquakes are cause away from plate boundaries. Non tectonic processes (eg fracking or mine subsidence) can cause local earthquakes and large explosions can also cause quakes by injecting energy into rocks. But why does this cause oscillatory shaking of the earth? Consider a much simpler case: a large bar of steel (maybe a rail from a railway). If you hit the bar with a hammer, you inject an increment of energy into the bar. But this does not cause just a single simple movement of the bar. It causes the bar to "ring" with frequencies characteristic of the material: the injection of energy is dissipated by vibrations in the bar. In solids there can be different types of vibration (a crude distinction is between compression waves like the transmission of sound in air and vibrational waves like the motion of a guitar string). The details are complicated in rigid solids but are easy to observe in simple systems. Basically when a rapid injection of energy happens in a solid: it vibrates as the energy is dissipated. The strong vibrations felt during an earthquake is simply a manifestation of those vibrations.

answer: Aphanitic means texture – crystals too small to see. Extrusive – formed at the surface (erupted lava/pyroclastics). Most extrusive rocks are volcanic, but some volcanic rocks are intrusive (subvolcanic) and can still be aphanitic because they cooled quickly at shallow depth. answer: Rotation is a strong agent in organising the fluid flows on Earth and other planets. As @jean-marie-prival already mentioned, this is largely due to the Coriolis force when you stand on the rotating planetary body. In the atmosphere, Coriolis force induces east & westward winds from north-south pressure gradients (as @john pointed out), curls local pressure low and high into cyclones (typhoons and hurricanes) and anticyclones, etc. In the ocean, Coriolis force also organises currents (e.g. geostrophic currents or in the form of Ekman transport ). It is so dominant in the atmospheric and oceanographic fluids that people developed special reduced models (e.g. quasi-geostrophic equations ) to describe the scenario where Coriolis force dominates. For the 3rd scenario you pointed out, rotation plays an even more important role in planetary magnetic field generation. In planetary dynamos (planetary fluids generating magnetic field), Coriolis force due to rotation wraps flow into helical columns (see e.g. wikipedia page on dynamo theory ). Modern simulations (e.g. Schaffer+ 2017 , picture below) confirm these columnar structures, signaling the dominating role of Coriolis force in the system. Same thing happens for virtually all simulations for planetary dynamos, be it on Earth, Jupiter or ice giants. The flow is always columnar, heavily controlled by rotation. That being said, if you sit on a constantly rotating body, Coriolis force itself cannot do work. Hence rotation cannot really drive fluid motion via Coriolis force, but only organise it or control it. Hence it must go hand in hand with convection or advection generated by other sources to modify the wind and current patterns, or generate magnetic field. It can also propagate waves (e.g. Rossby waves , inertial waves ), but again the waves are typically excited from sources other than rotation. Rotation alone can still drive fluid flow, but not in the form of Coriolis force. This occurs for instance when the rotation is not constant, but experiences changes over time, e.g. precession. Magnetic field generation through this non-constant-rotation driven flow is called precession-driven dynamo ( Tilger 2005 ) and to my knowledge is still quite an open question.

answer: No, because it is not magma buoyancy that drives eruptions. You are right in saying that buoyancy makes the magma rise from the mantle (where melt is produced) to the upper crust, where it is generally stored in a reservoir a few kilometers below the surface. But buoyancy is not the force at play during the last portion of the magma's journey. Instead, the force that drives an eruption is the exsolution and expansion of magmatic gases . The solubility of water (the main magmatic gas) diminishes with pressure. So, at some point the gas has to come out of the melt, taking more volume as a vapor phase, which pushes the mixture up and maintains the phenomenon (see also my answer here). Here is the beginning of the chapter " Magma Ascent and Degassing at Shallow Levels " from The Encyclopedia of Volcanoes : The most dramatic change that magma undergoes while ascending to the surface is volatile loss because of pressure drop. The process by which the silicate melt loses its dissolved volatile is called degassing. It is the main mechanism by which magma can reach the volcanic vent either as a mostly degassed lava that oozes quietly or as a fragmented mixture of gases and particles that explosively rushes out into the atmosphere. As to the factors limiting mountain growth, you can read the answers to " How high can a mountain possibly get? " In short, there is a theoretical limit due to gravity: if you keep adding mass to a mountain, at some point it will start to spread laterally or collapse, preventing it to reach a higher altitude. On Earth this limit is ~10 km, so Mauna Loa shouldn't be able to grow much further. Erosion could also play a role (glacial buzzsaw hypothesis), but this remains debated.
question: Are volcano heights limited by magma bouyancy?
question_context: There is a limit to how much pressure a volcano can erupt with. Magma chambers are under pressure from the surrounding solid rock. Lithostatic pressure as a function of depth is given by: $P_{rock} = \int \rho_{rock}(z)g(z) dz$ But rocks are solid and can hold shear forces. To be accurate, this formula needs to be taken using a reference point of "average terrain height" away from the volcano. Magma is less dense because it is liquid and contains water and other gases. These volatiles lower the melting point allowing overlying mantle rock to melt to a slush in the first place. This difference in densities drives volcanism. The limit to how high the lava can erupt is given by equating the pressure from the magma's own weight with that from the surrounding rock: $\int_{chamberfloor}^{refplane} \rho_{rock}(z)g(z) dz = \int_{chamberfloor}^{z_{summit}} \rho_{magma,gas}(z)g(z) dz$ . As the summit keeps getting higher and higher while the refplane at the base of the mountain stays constant, the RHS keeps growing but the LHS stays the same. When they are equal the bouncy can no longer overcome the weight of all the magma between the base and summit. answer: Prior to the evolution of life on earth, all soils, sands and sediments were the result of erosion. Much later, when oceans were established and life existed in the oceans, when lifeforms that had calcium carbonate died they fell to the floor of marine environments and over time their accumulation formed limestone. Prior to all this, very much prior to this, when the surface of the earth cooled and solidified, differential thermal stresses from heating and cooling resulted in the surface crystalline rock fragmenting, usually into individual mineral grains. This is the first form of erosion and the origin of the first soils, sands and sediments of earth. As the gaseous atmosphere development and the atmosphere experienced differential heating and cooling, winds formed. These picked up the fragments of crystalline material and moved it around, causing it to impact with unfragmented rock—in effect nature's original "sand blaster". This resulted in further erosion of surface rock and the creation of more soil, sand and sediment. When surface water arrived via comets, this resulted in the development of oceans, lakes, rivers and eventually rain. With the precipitation of rain, a third form of erosion was established. With the flow of surface waters, the eroded material was very easily transported into river deltas and water basins such as lakes and oceans.

answer: Amber does sink in Baltic seawater — the density gap means it never floats free. Three storm-linked mechanisms explain the seasonal pattern: Wave-orbital mobilization. Storm waves reach the seabed down to roughly the closure depth, lifting low-density particles like amber that fair-weather waves cannot move. Full-column mixing. Autumn and winter storms destroy the summer stratification, so mobilized particles are transported shoreward rather than resettling locally. Rafting with seagrass. Amber's density is close to that of waterlogged organic debris, so it strands together with the seaweed windrows that onshore storm winds pile onto beaches — which is exactly where experienced collectors search. Autumn/winter storms are roughly 6× more frequent than summer ones on the southern Baltic, which produces the seasonal concentration. Cold water does raise viscosity slightly (keeping stirred-up amber in suspension a bit longer), but the dominant term is storm frequency and energy, not buoyancy. answer: Ion size is playing a major role here. Calcium aluminate minerals do exist, as pointed out by the OP, but the calcium ion is too large to fit in the spinel structure. In turn, strontium and barium ions which are still larger do not fit well with the alternative mineral structures that calcium aluminate minerals form. Calcium monoaluminate occurs as the minerals krotite and dmitryivanovite , both with the formula $\ce{CaAl2O4}$ analogous to spinel. Krotite, the stable low-pressure form, is commonly associated with several other minerals including grossite, $\ce{CaAl4O7}$ (which, unlike the monoaluminates, has been found in terrestrial structures as well a meteorites) and spinel. Despite the analogous formula, the two monoaluminate minerals do not have the cubic spinel structure. In the case of krotite, the crystal structure is a "stuffed tridymite" structure [ 1 ], in which the calcium ions occupy interstitial sites in a relatively open network. Strontium or barium, within even larger than calcium and would not fit either this structure or the spinel one. More generally, the larger size of the calcium ion, compared with other +2 metal ions most commonly found in rocks, leads to the formation of entirely different mineral structures. Such mineral structures tend to be less dense than minerals built with magnesium ions which tend to intermingle with the heavier fourth-period transition elements. This property goes along with calcium having a relatively high abundance in Earth's crust rather than the mantle. Reference Ma, C., Kampf, A. R., Connolly, H. C., Beckett, J. R., Rossman, G. R., Smith, S. A. S., & Schrader, D. L. (2011). "Krotite, CaAl2O4, a new refractory mineral from the NWA 1934 meteorite". answer: Using space-time clustering to define whole seismic regions is probably going to give you weird results, because in seismology, space-time clustering is actually used to separate foreshocks and aftershocks from the background earthquakes. We call this declustering. When a huge earthquake hits, like the 2011 Tohoku or 2004 Sumatra quakes, it sets off thousands of aftershocks in a very tight area and time window. If you run a standard space-time clustering algorithm on that Kaggle dataset, your clusters are just going to be those massive aftershock sequences rather than actual tectonic regions. Then, if you calculate the Gutenberg-Richter b-value on those clusters, you're just measuring the b-value of a specific aftershock sequence, which behaves completely differently from a whole region's long-term background seismicity. If you want to compare regions, you generally have to decluster the catalog first using something like the Gardner-Knopoff or Zaliapin-Ben-Zion method so the aftershocks don't skew your stats, or at least use pure spatial clustering while keeping in mind that tectonic faults are long and linear, so algorithms like k-means that look for round blobs will chop fault lines up in unnatural ways (DBSCAN or hierarchical clustering works way better for fault geometry). You are honestly much better off using established seismic zones so you are comparing apples to apples. The classic global standard is the Flinn-Engdahl regionalization, which splits the world into 754 geographic and seismic zones and is already built into a lot of USGS data. Another great option is the GEM (Global Earthquake Model) source zones, or even just downloading the Peter Bird (2003) tectonic plate boundary shapefiles and grouping the earthquakes by which type of boundary they sit on, like subduction zones versus mid-ocean ridges. A really cool project for a stats student would actually be to take the Flinn-Engdahl or Bird plate regions, calculate your b-values there, and then compare that to what you get when you let a spatial algorithm like DBSCAN draw the borders based purely on epicenters and depth. Just make sure you check the completeness magnitude ( $M_c$ ) of the dataset before doing any b-value math, though that specific Kaggle dataset is mostly M5.5+ from 1965 onwards, so it should be mostly complete except maybe in the 1960s in the southern hemisphere.

answer: As with a lot of things in medicine, balance is important. Short answer: A wound kept in a moist environment will generally heal faster than in a dry environment, however, excessive moisture can have negative impacts. Maintaining the ideal moist environment is likely more important in earlier stages of wound healing. N.B. Where there is no journal reference present, information is likely sourced from UpToDate , specifically the Principles of Acute Wound Management article. Long answer: Immediately after cutting yourself When you cut yourself, your body first tries to stop the bleeding. This is the clotting that usually occurs in the first few minutes. At this point, the only important feature of the dressing is that it is helping stop the bleeding, to allow the actual healing to take place later. Almost any clean dressing that can be used to provide gentle pressure and prevent infection is suitable at this point. During infection If the wound is infected, it will typically become inflamed as part of the immune response. During this stage, actual healing is mostly inhibited so the most important factor is helping the body fight the infection, so aren't really relevant to your question. In recovery Moist environment When left to the air to dry out, your wounds will form the darkened and dry scab you mentioned. While a scab can sometimes do a decent job in protecting the wound from infection or further damage, as well as stopping bleeding, it inhibits the regeneration of epithelium (the top layer of skin). In a moist environment, such as one maintained by an occlusive dressing (water/air tight dressing) wounds typically heal significantly faster, and with possibly reduced scarring. Wounds need water, nutrients and a bunch of signalling molecules to heal. Maintaining the moist environment of the wound ensures that these are all available to the regrowing cells. This is where the advice to keep it moist would be coming from. There is a large amount of evidence on this, starting from the original 1962 paper , tested on pigs due to medical ethics, which found a notably faster rate of regrowth in moist environments. 98% of wounds in the moist environment healed 3 days, whereas only 37% of those in the dry had healed by then; infact it took until 7 days for a similar fraction (100%) to have healed. In dry environments, the scab was also noticed to block the regrowth of skin cells back over the wound area. This 1995 study is one of many others reinforcing the originals ideas, and again demonstrating that dry wounds heal slower. Dry environment However, you can end up with excess moisture, either exudate from the wound itself, or from external sources (eg. getting the dressing wet) which can both hinder healing: It can lead to maceration , skin degeneration/decay due to excess moisture being aborbed into the skin. This excess moisture can also promote bacterial/fungal growth. The wrinkles you get from the bath are caused by the same absorption of excess moisture into skin, though over the timescale of a bath, are perfectly safe. External moisture (ie. getting the wound wet while it is not in a waterproof/resistant dressing) can provide an access point for bacteria or dirt. If this leads to an infection, then swelling, wound healing is delayed. Getting the wound wet can wash out some of the beneficial molecules that encourage cell regrowth, as well those needed to create new tissue, delaying healing. Furthermore, tissue requires oxygen to regrow, and leaving it open to air allows for plentiful supply. These are likely where the arguements to keep the wound dry came from. Finding balance The typical best practice is to keep wounds moist with their own fluid, or saline solution if they are already drier, bandaged with a dressing that : Keeps moisture around the wound Absorbs or allows the evaportion excess exudate (moisture) produced by the wound Prevents bacteria/dirt entry Protects the wound from further damage Allows oxygen in to help healing And to monitor, at regular changes, signs of maceration (ie. very white/soft skin) and allowing it some time to air out/dry if this happens. This would usually look like the bandages you are familiar with, to keep the wound moist , while seperately keeping the bandage dry (or using a waterproof dressing) to avoid other issues. As recovery progresses and the wound closes with skin (not a scab) the importance of maintainig moisture diminishes.

answer: TL;DR - The hepatitis C virus (HCV) is transmitted by blood-to-blood exposure, not casual exposure. According to the CDC : HCV is transmitted primarily through exposures to infectious blood. Possible exposures include: Injection drug use (currently the most common mode of HCV transmission in the US) Birth from an HCV-infected person. Although less frequent, HCV can also be spread through: Sex with an HCV-infected person (although uncommon, HIV-infected men who have sex with men have an increased risk of sexual transmission). Sharing personal items contaminated with infectious blood, such as razors or toothbrushes. Other invasive health care procedures that involve injections. Unregulated tattooing and piercing. Donated blood, blood products, and organs (rare in the US since blood screening became available in 1992). Needlestick injuries in health care settings. So it would be extremely unlikely that you could become infected by dried blood on a book or other inanimate object. I can imagine scenarios where it could happen, but they really stretch the boundaries of credibility. Remember also that infection requires a sufficient viral load, and doing something like touching a spot of dried blood with a minor wound on your finger would be unlikely to transfer enough virus to cause infection. Exposure to dried blood simply isn't how transmission happens. Incidentally, I don't know what you think dried blood looks like, but dried blood is usually black, not red. answer: At the membrane, an electrical potential is build via two independent processes: K_ir proteins (stands for inwardly racrifying potassium channel) and other K+ leak channels let positively charged potassium ions diffuse towards the cell. The Na+/K+-ATPase protein (sodium-potassium-pump) exchanges 3 sodium ions from the inside against 2 potassium ions from the outside, both against their concentration gradient. One of the main functions of the membrane is keeping other ions from moving either way so that an electrochemical equilibrium is maintained: a lot of K+ inside the cell (high concentration) hinder more K+ ions to continue to leak in because the chemical gradient is producing a force towards the outside of the cell. On the other hand, there also is an electrical gradient due to a lot of active proteins that are anions, negatively charged ions, inside the cell. Those are way to big for any diffusion, though, facilitated or not. Thus, the inside is more negatively charged than the outside: the resting potential of the membrane. The push factor of the chemical gradient (more K+ inside the cell) and the pull factor of the electrical gradient (inside of the cell negatively charged) equal each other out while other ions are blocked from passing. That's what makes the resting potential relatively stable. That being said, there are some channels for negatively charged ions, mainly Cl- channels, that exist. For a more or less short amount of time, they let Cl- ions flush into the cell (the extracellular concentration is way higher in most cases, they follow along a high chemical gradient). This lowers the excitability of, e.g., neurons, because the electrical gradient becomes greater: instead of the electrical gradient, the high chemical gradient is the main driver. It produces a much higher drag into the cell despite the electrical gradient going the other way, just because the Cl- concentration is so much lower inside the cell. Thus, I think the main problem in your train of thought is that you only think in terms of electrical gradients and individual ions that shall equal each other out, while the big picture is about an electrochemical equilibrium of forces/gradients and the sum of ions over time. In reality, there is constant, if slow, exchange along gradients and back all the time. Nothing in living cells is static and the membrane should be imagined rather like a pontoon bridge than a wall. answer: When you breathe out and back in, you replace the gas in your lungs with the gas in the outside air. The lungs have a high surface area interface between blood gas and lung gas and function to make the partial pressures of gases in the lungs and blood nearly equal. Importantly, you do not use up all the oxygen in the lungs between breaths. To do so, you'd have to also use up all the oxygen in the blood: remember that the lungs make the partial pressures nearly equal. Typical partial pressures of oxygen in the atmosphere are around 160 Torr, lungs around 100 Torr, arterial blood around 100 Torr, venous blood around 50 Torr. See for example Wikipedia Pulmonary Gas Pressures . If you hold your breath, then the total oxygen in your body is the amount dissolved in the blood and all the tissues and the amount in the lungs. You'll eventually use this up in metabolism, and when the partial pressure of oxygen drops sufficiently you will eventually lose consciousness, but this is relatively slow. If you breathe an inert gas like nitrogen, every breath is a pump taking the amount of oxygen in the lungs and replacing it with zero oxygen. The lungs then will fill with some oxygen from the blood before the next breath, at which point it will all be pumped out again.

answer: There is no "rigorous science" behind the claim. Whether Tylenol/acetaminophen (N- a cetyl- p ara- a mino p henol/APAP) causes autism has been looked at in many studies, but there has not been any solid evidence to date that it does , while the opposite, that APAP does not cause autism, has been borne out in some good studies. There are a number of studies that show APAP use may contribute to "neurodevelopmental problems" (ADHD and other conditions) later in life, but the vast majority of studies are flawed. First, they mostly rely on memory/self reporting, which is notoriously problematic. Another is that the reason women might take APAP during pregnancy, e.g. for fever, pain, or conditions which are painful (e.g. arthritis/other inflammatory conditions) may be the causative factor itself, as opposed to the pain meds. Again, this is a very difficult confounding factor. Another issue is the genetics of autism. What we do know about autism is that there is a strong genetic component; studies are starting to locate genes associated with (?responsible for) the condition. Studies of twins and siblings have shown that the incidence of autism spectrum disorder in identical twins is as high as 90%, and in siblings, either dizygotic twins or separate pregnancies, it's as high as 30%. Autism is also somewhat dependent on environmental factors, e.g. the family the child is born into and the exposures it may have. That's another problem with most of the studies; it's difficult to determine the association of autism with medication use because subjects and controls are raised in different environments which cannot be controlled for. So, unless the controls are raised in the same environment (impossible for non-sibling controls), the causation cannot be proven for APAP use. The largest and best study, was published last year in the Journal of the American Medical Association. It is a Swedish study with over 2.4 million children. The study attempted to compensate for the lack of controls most studies are plagued with by using sibling-matched controls, and found no evidence of increased incidence of autism with APAP use. There is a higher incidence of autism in circumcised males, but is that because of the pain associated with the procedure or with the analgesic administered for post-surgical pain? That's not a minor point. All types of pain in neonates, especially preemies, is associated with a higher incidence of neurodevelopmental disorders. The use of analgesics in such cases is ubiquitous. Which factor caused what? Corellation does not equal causation. To do a proper study, one would need to have a group of boys get post-circumcision APAP, and another group to be denied APAP, or to receive a more dangerous analgesic or local anesthesia/nerve block, and follow those infants for 10 years. However, any use of APAP during infancy for any reason would would confound the results.
