answer: Overview of Cancer All nucleated cells in the body have means of proliferation (by proto-oncogenes ) and deliberate self-induced death (by tumor suppressors ), which they regulate according to their functions; for example, a cell in the lining of the esophagus proliferates rapidly, while neurons have typically all but ceased their proliferation in adulthood. When genes that induce cell death and prevent proliferation, or the products of those genes, are altered (for instance due to a mutation), there's a likelihood that the cell may enter an endless cycle of proliferation. This is a cell in its so-called precancerous state that can quickly, or slowly, become fully cancerous. A real-life example is p53 , a tumor suppressor protein, loss of whose function, often due to a mutation in the gene encoding it, is implicated in the pathology of half of all known cancers [1]. Once a cell is cancerous, unless identified and removed by the immune system, which happens in >99% of the cases, it deviates more and more from normal ones as the cancer progresses. It will cease to perform normal tissue function, and instead devote all the resources it can muster to an increasingly faulty mitosis. In doing so, it will utilize many cellular pathways involved in signaling the cell to proliferate. A series of these pathways involve remodeling tissue structure, something our body normally does constantly in response to the shear and tear that frequently happens in epithelia across the body. SERPINB3, a Biomarker of Cancer The principle guiding diagnosis and treatment, whether of cancer or skin warts, is to target molecules and processes the disruption of which would cause minimal damage to healthy cells while effectively removing the undesired ones. If you do achieve this ideal, you will have cured that cancer type. To diagnose a certain type of cancer, a circulating molecule was found to be sensitive and specific, and thus a suitable biomarker, and after a few name changes, was named SERPINB3 [2,3]. SERPINB3 is a serine proteinase inhibitor involved in tissue remodeling, among its other roles [2]. In simple terms, if the linings of the tissues in the body are some sort of fabric, the body uses other fabric, tailor's knives, scissors, and sheaths to shape the fabric in specific ways. SERPINB3 is a sheath. Cancerous cells employ the body's "tailoring tools", including SERPINB3, to remodel the tissue so they would take up more space and invade lymph nodes. The levels of SERPINB3 in circulation thus increase in certain cancer types, enabling (early) diagnosis to guide clinical decisions forward. SERPINB3 in Wound Healing Process To sum up the previous section, what happened, chronologically, is that the levels of a certain protein in the blood were found to have been increased in a certain cancer type, suggesting that tracking its levels was a useful way of diagnosing that cancer type. Since then, this target has been found to be a useful diagnostic marker in several other cancers as well. Its gene was described, and several roles for it had been identified. The main role for SERPINB3 in the body had been elusive, however, and that's what's been the focus of the new study by Yaron et al. After harmful debris left by a wound is cleaned up by the immune system, re-epithelization is the process during which new epithelium restores tissue integrity in the skin [4]. It is initiated by the activation and migration of keratinocytes to the site of the wound, and the authors propose that SERPINB3 plays a pivotal role in stimulating this process. As has been explained above, the role of SERPINB3 in re-epithelization is not incongruous with its role in cancer. SERPINB3, in healthy tissue as well as cancerous ones, acts as a cog in the complex machinery involved in remodeling and modifying tissue. Whether targeting it to enhance the wound healing process in various disease states such as chronic ulcers would be viable is not a question the study answers, and further research is needed to explore such possibilities, which would depend on a myriad of factors pertinent to the feasibility of any such endeavor, which are too broad to delve into in an answer here. So to;dr: melena is a distinct entity, dependent on site, volume and amount of time spent in the GI tract. answer: This is a very interesting question! The most critical difference between a male and female heart is the size and ventricular load. Although the physiological characteristics of a heart can and do adapt to the donor's body, there are certainly limitations to this function. Prior to modern predictions of left-ventricular mass using imaging technology, opposite-sex transplants often lead to heart failure. For female hearts being transplanted to a male's body, any significant size difference (which is relatively common due to the 25%~ lower average size of the female heart) could lead to overstretching of cardiomyocytes in the heart due to the higher blood volume per stroke necessary in a male cardiovascular system. "..compared to the male heart, the female heart has a larger ejection fraction and beats at a faster rate but generates a smaller cardiac output." (ref1) The gendered electrophysiology of the heart is primarily dependent on hormonal signaling. As this suggests, testosterone production will cause the electrophysiology of the heart to adapt. answer: is it possible to concentrate enough charge in a small region of space such that an electron wouldn't be able to escape unless it were moving at the speed of light — effectively creating an electric-field-based analog of a black hole, not due to gravity but due to the strength of the electric field? No. Not in the same sense that gravitational fields create black holes. An "electric-field based black hole" you'd think would require massive electrical forces, but when electric fields approach or exceed the Schwinger limit $$V=\frac{m_e^2c^3}{q_e\hbar}\approx 1.32\times 10^{18}\ Vm^{-1}$$ then QFT effects become significant. At such intense electric fields, there will be spontaneous electron-positron pair production , which will quench the electric field making it short-lived. It is not a question of whether we can have an electric field strong enough to prevent electrons from escaping (like a black hole does for light), but more that quantum electrodynamic effects fundamentally set an upper bound on how strong a continued electric field can be . Edit: good point made in comment by Yukterez . It is generally accepted that electromagnetic energy with extremely high intensities will exert a repulsive gravitational force. answer: My doubt arises about how people can create these ideal concepts when nothing to date has even been ideal, and how exactly are concepts of ideality useful if it doesn't correspond with what's going on in real life? The answer to the "how" here is on the face of it quite simple: we make observations, analyze the data, and accordingly build mathematical models that describe it. Simplifying assumptions are useful because in many cases what determines our ability to solve an equation is precisely such a simplifying assumption. Anyone who went through introductory mechanics knows the example of how the small angle approximation allows us to find an (approximate) solution to the motion of a simple pendulum that was slightly displaced. Whether the idealizations are useful is also ultimately decided by experiment: in the case of the pendulum, we indeed find that for small displacements, its motion (to a good degree of accuracy) is described by the "idealized" equation for a simple harmonic oscillator. The same principle holds for many other common idealizations, like the assumption that the rope is massless, that there is no friction at the pivot, no air resistance, etc. More often than not then, we find that such simplifications are useful, and a lot can be learned by studying the system under such simplifying assumptions first , before adding in all the nitty gritty complications of reality. Physicists "like" this reductionistic approach, because it proves useful time and again, and allows focusing on a specific aspect of nature they want to study, while putting aside for the time being (as much as possible) what's of less relevance to the subject matter. Of course, that's not always possible, and additional complications may have to be added to our existing models when we find that these become too significant to neglect. But that's good -- because that means we also get to find out the domain of validity of each such "idealized" model that we invent. We always want to push a model to its edge where we are absolutely sure it breaks down; then that's the point we know we need to work from in discovering a more general model. But we don't want to waste time on "fixing a thing that ain't broken", so to speak, so we "hold on" to a model as long as we possibly can in that sense. Wouldn't it make better sense to skip the ideality? Equations that can be directly proved by real-life results? Instead of imagining the blocks sliding in my head, I could just measure the roughness of the table at different points, account for the variables, and, to a certain accuracy, calculate the forces and velocities correctly. That would defeat the entire point of physics, and in fact of any science. The point of science, to quote Richard Feynman is " to tell you about an experiment that hasn't been done ". If all you do is only describe what goes on in a directly observed experiment, then this is merely a mechanical, descriptive endeavor, which doesn't add anything to our fundamental understanding of how nature works. We are interested to find the basic laws from which all the complex variety of natural phenomena arises. To do that, we do indeed require a lot imagination, and mathematical sophistication; measurement devices are crucial, but are not sufficient to achieve that goal. So under a lab setting, parameters can be tweaked and controlled. smoothness of the table, force used for pulling, the materials, all that. So instead of thinking about a ideal scenario that never exists/will never exist, we could have varied a parameter each time and made an observation and made laws and equations that follow actual experimental observation. that would have been easier to approximate them into simpler equations which still provide a rather accurate solution. Well that sounds nice, and to a large degree we do that in gathering experimental data. But in some cases it just won't do. For example, can we do anything in our labs to help us understand the nature of dark energy? What parameter can we "tweak" to reproduce the conditions near a black hole's event horizon? How will a lab setting help us investigate the anomalous rotation curves of distant galaxies? It turns out with all these things that it's not so simple to just " approximate them into simpler equations ", much less so in cases where we have no control over the environmental parameters; we just often have to make do with what nature provides us with. But to see an example of when your general idea is indeed useful, take the notable case of how Planck deduced what's now known as Planck's law , describing blackbody radiation in thermal equilibrium. Now in the process of working out the law itself, and by making some heuristically motivated assumptions, Planck was able to compute what we now call "Planck's constant". At first this constant was not interwoven into the framework of the rest of physics, and Planck himself considered it a mere mathematical artefact. Only later theoretical work, by Einstein and others, involving a lot of imagination and working from conceptual physical principles, led us to understand how Planck's constant plays a role in much more than just the specific phenomenon of black body radiation. It would have been a very sad thing if, discovering such a constant, we would not have pursued and discovered its connection to other parts of physics, like the energy quantization of photons, angular momentum, etc. So you see that even when we find a mathematical pattern from just an apparently isolated phenomenon, we immediately try to generalize it and understand its place in the bigger picture of nature. We do that simply because we find time and again that it is useful, in that it is a sure way to find more general laws with enhanced predictive power. Here I can end then with another, very relevant quote by Richard Feynman: Nature uses only the longest threads to weave her patterns, so each small piece of her fabric reveals the organization of the entire tapestry.

answer: Does a rotating universe need a center? No. A canonical example is the Gödel metric. This is a solution of Einstein equations for dust matter with a negative cosmological constant. It is a homogeneous spacetime, so every point of it looks like any other point. So there is neither unique “center of the universe” nor unique axis of rotation but it is not isotropic : at each point there is a distinguished (spatial) direction, local axis of rotation. An observer in comoving frame would see all the matter in the Universe rigidly rotate around him with constant angular velocity as if he was at the center of the Universe. But any other comoving observer at any point in spacetime would have the same experience! Of course, Gödel universe is stationary, so there is no expansion and thus it could not model our Universe. It is also pathological: it contains closed timelike curves through every point of the spacetime. But the second of Gödel's GR papers (from 1952) provides examples of universes that have both expansion and rotation. This paper ( here is a reprinted version from 2000 ) is less well known than the one from 1949 (describing the Gödel metric), so let's review properties of such solutions. As could be expected from Newtonian reasoning, with expansion the angular velocity of rotation slows. Of course, such universe is no longer homogeneous spacetime but it is spatially homogeneous (as a cosmological model), at a given moment of cosmic time, any spatial point looks like any other and every comoving observer will still see universe rotating as a whole, with him as the center. Expansion can also possibly cure pathologies of the Gödel's metric and if rotation is small enough such spacetime can be arbitrarily close to nonrotating isotropic cosmological solutions. So if observations are compatible with isotropic non-rotating cosmological model they would also be compatible with rotating (anisotropic) cosmology given small enough rotation. Thus such solutions can conceivably describe our Universe. Answers to a previous question What if the universe is rotating as a whole? hint at the possibility of having an axis of rotation but delocalized over space (always located at the observer). How is this possible? Equivalence principle. If all the matter in the universe is rotating around one point under the influence of gravity alone, then trajectory of each matter particle would corresponds to a local inertial frame and could serve as new center of rotation. This is straightforward generalization of rigid body kinematics where the angular velocity of rotation is independent on the choice of origin. Also this is analogous to kinematics of the uniform expansion of the universe, where every comoving observes sees himself at a center of expansion.

answer: The Short Answer: Total Internal Reflection. These circular shadows are formed by the rings of reflected light bouncing off the water's surface and illuminating the bottom of the pool. The Long Answer: Since the lamps are embedded in the bottom of the pool, they emit light only upwards. Therefore, there is no need for an obstruction to cause a shadow: they just don't shine on the bottom of the pool. In fact, if the pool were drained, the bottom of the (now dry) pool would be entirely dark because all the light would escape upwards into the night sky. So the real question is not "Why are there shadows?" but rather "Why are there rings of light surrounding those shadows?". The rings of light form due to reflections off the surface of the water bouncing back down towards the bottom of the pool. When light passes from one medium (like water) into another (like air), it bends in a process called refraction following a rule known as Snell's Law . However, not all of the light escapes the first medium; some of the light reflects off the boundary between the media (usually following the so-called "law of reflection" ). However, when light travels from a denser medium (i.e. water) into a less dense medium (i.e. air), the overwhelming majority of the light will be transmitted (and very little will be reflected) so long as the light hits the boundary at an angle sufficiently close to perpendicular. However, beyond a special angle called the critical angle , the vast majority of the light will be reflected in a process known as "total internal reflection" which prevents the light from escaping into the air. In this case, the large, round shadow is caused by a ring of reflected light bouncing off the bottom of the water's surface and illuminating the bottom of the pool. As an interesting side note: The diameter of the circular shadow can be used to experimentally determine the index of refraction of the water using the following diagram: where $d$ is the diameter of the light, $D$ is the diameter of the shadow, $h$ is the depth of the water, and $\theta$ is the critical angle. Assuming the index of refraction of air to be approximately $1$ (i.e. indistinguishable from a vacuum), then a little bit of trigonometry results in the following formula for the index of refraction of the water: $n=\sqrt{1+(\frac{4h}{D+d})^2}$ . I've measured this pool and know that the water has a depth of around $h=10.125 \text{ in.}$ , the lamps are about $d=3 \text{ in.}$ across, and the little tiles on the bottom of the pool are about $2 \text{ in.}$ on a side (which implies that the shadows in this picture are approximately $D=46 \text{ in.}$ wide). This gives us an experimental index of refraction of water of $n=1.297$ . This number agrees to two significant figures with the standard, accepted index of refraction for water. Not bad! As a final comment: Some careful thought will also show that $D+d$ must be a constant of the system, so a point source of light would have a shadow of diameter $D+d$ ( $49 \text{ in.}$ ) while a giant lamp of diameter $\frac{D+d}{2}$ ( $24.5 \text{ in.}$ ) would have no shadow at all.

It's possible the force diagram looks something more like this: If you tilt the object even more, the person at the lower end can carry the entire weight of the object, with the person at the top end contributing arbitrarily little horizontal force to keep the object from toppling over. The point of application of force will also have an effect for real objects with thickness, even if force is applied directly upwards. Consider what happens when two people carry a box down stairs, picking it up in the usual fashion by the bottom corners. As the box tilts, the lower person's corner gets closer to the center of mass and the upper person's corner gets farther - to balance the torque, the lower person must exert a greater force than the upper one: This doesn't happen when considering an idealized flat object, but it certainly makes a difference when carrying real things. As yet one more explanation for why something might feel heavier when lifting to different heights, this scenario often occurs when carrying something up or down a slope or stairs, not just when two people of different heights carry something on level ground. To get the object moving up the stairs or to stop it at the bottom, the total upward force must be greater than the object's weight - when carrying something up or down a slope, there may be a point at which both parties carry more than half the weight!

In fact, the first measurements of current in the 1820’s predate both Faraday’s law (1831) and Ampere’s law (1850s), which predate Maxwell’s equations (1865). Similarly, measurements of mass and distance and time predate Newton’s development of the theory of mechanics. There may be exceptions, where the theory predated the measurements, but they are not the rule. History is messy, and science is iterative. Primitive measurement devices (predating the theory) are grouped by agreement with each other, often by agreement with some seminal experiment. Practical experience is gained through further experiments. These eventually lead to refined designs that are more precise and reproducible, as well as a deeper understanding of the measurand. This deeper understanding of the measurand can then lead to the development of a theory. And then the theory can be used to develop more refined measurement devices. Often the more refined measurement devices use a different physical principle than the original device. But they are recognized as measuring the same measurand by the fact that they agree with the original device within some suitable domain of operation. The fact that measurement devices are classified and grouped based on agreement with each other persists even after the relevant theory is developed, and even if the relevant theory changes. For example, despite the fact that they use very different mechanisms, sundials, pendulum clocks, hourglasses, pocket watches, quartz oscillators, and atomic clocks are all clocks because they all agree with each other. This categorization existed before Newton’s theory of mechanics was developed and after the Newtonian understanding of time was replaced by relativity. Fundamentally, it is this agreement that categorizes a type of measurement device and defines the measurand. The associated theory is not essential to that categorization.

answer: Quantum theory can be applied to finite number of particles (quantum mechanics) or to fields (quantum theory of fields). The application to particles is mathematically easier and the resulting mathematical theory is simpler. The most important unresolved mysteries of quantum theory pop up already when we apply it to particles - when/how the quantum state collapse happens, what is/when is measurement, when a definite result can be obtained in a measurement, why that particular result happens, why the Born rule works, tensions with the original ideas of relativity (Bell's non-locality). We may call these mysteries shortly as "what is really going on". QFT is a result of the efforts to apply quantum theory to fields - systems with infinite number of degrees of freedom. It provides some new picture of the world and new mathematics, but just as the quantum theory of particles, it answers only a very limited range of experience-related questions, e.g. probabilities of results of scattering events or average values of physical quantities. It seems to me that only a small fraction of people interested in those old mysteries refer to QFT. Maybe only similarly small fraction expects that QFT is likely to provide something new and useful to resolution of those mysteries. Why is that? The study of the old mysteries is mostly about finding and carefully evaluating the logically possible alternatives to / completions of the orthodox quantum theory that would result in a consistent picture of how the world works, in agreement with known empirical results. Those empirical results are not only the confirmations of the quantum theory predictions (statistics of results), but also the non-statistical facts, e.g. the fact we get a definite macroscopic outcome in a single experiment, the fact of single particle creating a single spot on the detecting screen, classical physics working so well, possible presence and effects of gravity, etc. These are hard things to resolve within a single theory already when using quantum theory of particles. QFT, although incorporating ideas of special relativity and bringing in spacetime-based description of the world, does not seem to offer much practical advantage in formulating and solving the old mysteries. The Born rule is applied in a similar way as in the quantum theory of particles; no new insight into its origin is found. No revelation on collapse or entanglement came from QFT. No quantum theory of gravitational field had much success. Maybe this is because QFT, historically, is a result of a particular way of developing the quantum theory, which could and did proceed without a careful consideration of the old mysteries of quantum theory, without refining the concept of measurement and without any commitment to a unique consequential picture of "what is really going on". Orthodox quantum theory, including QFT, may be seen as the crown jewel of the "shut up and calculate" approach. It is the major supporting case for that methodological attitude in physics which says one can get quite far, and obtain quite a lot of useful results, with the formulaic/formalistic approach, which applies the old ideas and rules of quantum theory (such as the commutation relations, the unitary evolution, the Born rule) to new situations, new kinds of systems or new sets of mathematical constraints. All this can be done and seems to largely have been done without a substantial refining of the fundamental concept of measurement and without a unique picture of "what is really going on". So it should not be surprising that QFT, just as the quantum theory of particles, does not provide much insight into those old mysteries.

answer: The point of the ZPE is not that it is non-zero, because that could indeed be undone by redefining the potential energy as $$ V\rightarrow \overline{V}=V-E_0 \ . $$ The resulting potential energy has now a somewhat unintuitive dependence on $\hbar$ , but the new ZPE is indeed $\overline{E}_0=0$ . However, the important thing is not whether $E_0$ or $\overline{E}_0$ is zero or not, but that the difference $E_0-V_\text{min}=\overline{E}_0-\overline{V}_\text{min}$ is greater than zero, where $V_\text{min}=V(\vec{r}_\text{min})$ . This has the important meaning that a particle in an energy eigenstate cannot be strictly localized in the mimimum of the potential (or in its arbitrarily small neighborhood), and this is where the usual arguments with the uncertainty principle come into play. There is obviously no such restriction in classical mechanics, where a particle could be standing still in $\vec{r}_\text{min}$ with zero kinetic energy. This may not seem such a big deal for the harmonic oscillator, but consider instead a hydrogen atom, where the minimum of the potential energy is either $-\infty$ or a very large negative number, depending on whether a point-like or a small finite nucleus is assumed. The zero line of the energy could be again shifted in any way, but the shift-invariant $E_0-V_\text{min}>0$ means that the electron cannot fall into the nucleus. (This just means that the electron cannot be strictly localized at the nucleus with a delta-function-like density, not that it does not have detection probability at that region; actually, $S$ -states always have a non-zero detection probability around the nucleus.)
question: Is zero-point energy a mathematical artifact?

This feels natural - I've always been slightly puzzled by the existence of the zero-point energy $\frac{\omega}{2}$ for the quantum harmonic oscillator. Yet the math seemed 'obvious' to me, until today. Let $H$ , $a$ and $a^\dagger$ be the Hamiltonian, annihilation and creation operators, respectively, defined by: $$H = \frac{1}{2}(p^2 + \omega^2 x^2)$$ $$a = \frac{x}{\sqrt{2\omega}} + i\sqrt{\frac{\omega}{2}}p.$$ Then one can find the following relations: $$H = \omega(a^\dagger a + \frac{1}{2})$$ $$H|n\rangle = (n + \frac{1}{2})\omega|n\rangle$$ Where $|n\rangle$ is the $n$ 'th eigenstate of $H$ . This gives a zero point energy (ZPE) of $\omega / 2$ . So far so good. Yet today I was reading David Tong's lecture notes on QFT. In the second chapter, he makes the remark that classically: $$H_{\text{classical}} = \frac{1}{2}(p^2 + \omega^2 x^2) = \frac{1}{2}(\omega x - ip)(\omega x + ip).$$ Let $H'$ be the quantum analogue of the right hand side expression. Then: $$H' = \frac{1}{2}(\omega x - ip)(\omega x + ip) = \omega a^\dagger a$$ $$H' = H - \frac{1}{2}\omega.$$ Thus yielding a different Hamiltonian operator, due to the fact that $x$ and $p$ do not commute. In particular, the ZPE is zero for $H'$ : $$H'|0\rangle = (H - \frac{1}{2}\omega)|0\rangle = 0.$$ I understand the Hamiltonian operator is ultimately defined as the generator of time evolution. There seems to be no difference between $H$ and $H'$ in that regard. Why is there a preference for $H$ over $H'$ in QM textbooks? And is this notion of strictly non-zero ZPE, which is often linked to the uncertainty principle, incorrect? What are the consequences for our interpretation of QM phenomena if the ZPE is indeed arbitrary? EDIT: Thanks for all your responses. It's clear to me now that I was confusing zero-point energy and zero-point motion.

answer: The larger droplets are older i.e. they formed first as small droplets then grew by coalescence or ripening to become bigger. The smaller droplets are smaller because they formed later and haven't had a chance to grow. Water droplets on a surface nucleate at a critical size that depends on the water-surface interfacial energy. The reason for this is that while condensation reduces the water energy by the latent heat of condensation it also increases the energy due to the water/surface and water/air interfacial energies. For more on this see my answer to Why condensation nuclei is required for condensation and formation of clouds? or the Wikipedia article on the critical radius . Once a droplet has formed it is energetically favourable for it to grow as that reduces the area:volume ratio and hence reduces the interfacial energy relative to the energy released by condensation. Exactly what happens will depend on the surface, but on glass typically the nuclei grow by condensation from the gas phase until they touch other droplets and coalesce with them. The obvious next question is why did the oldest drops nucleate closest to the edge of the window i.e. why do the drops become younger as we move away from the edge towards the centre of the window? Typically this happens because heat loss is greatest at the window frame so the glass nearest the frame is cooled the most. If you measured the temperature of the glass you should see a temperature gradient as you move away from the frame.

answer: Thermoception is a topic in psychophysics (or more broadly, in biophysics). We generally perceive heat flux rather than temperature directly, as animal thermoceptors signal in response to skin temperature changes. However, heat flux (and hence skin temperature changes) depend on other physical factors than just air temperature. The heat flux is lower if the air is still and higher in wind (as the flow forcibly drives convection and disrupts an insulating boundary layer). The effectiveness of perspiration (to evaporatively dissipate waste metabolic heat from an animal's body) is reduced by ambient humidity, that is, by elevated wet bulb temperature. (These factors impact not just subjective sensation but also alter the survivability of extreme environments, for example wind chill affects rate of frostbite injury onset and wet bulb temperature predictions are important in placing an upper limit to human adaptability to climate change.) In meteorology, a formula is used to account for these other physical factors that influence temperature perception, for example the Australian Bureau of Meteorology has used what is known as the Steadman Apparent Temperature : $$T' = T_a + 0.33e - 0.70v - 4.00$$ Here, $T_a$ is the ambient air temperature (°C), $e$ is the atmospheric water vapour pressure (hPa), and $v$ is the near-surface wind speed (m/s). (The constant term represents how the body loses heat more easily than normal in air that is unusually dry.)

answer: Can a "beat frequency"...cause the room to resonate? No. Beat frequency is an illusion. "Beat frequency" is part of a story about how we perceive sounds. When you play two different notes at the same time, the waveform that reaches your ear simply is the sum of the two individual note waveforms. The "beat" that you hear can be explained by referring to the Prosthephaeresis identities . In plain English: The Sum of two pure sine waves is mathematically indistinguishable from a single, pure tone whose frequency is half-way between the two real frequencies, and whose amplitude is modulated by a sinusoid whose frequency is half the difference between the two real frequencies. That amplitude modulation is what your ears perceive as the "beat." Looking at it from the other direction, if you set up an analog music synthesizer to send the output of a sine-wave VFO tuned to audio frequency, A, through amplitude modulation by a control voltage that is a much slower sine wave of frequency C; and if you feed the output into an audio spectrum analyzer, you will see neither frequency A nor frequency C in the spectrum.* Instead, you will see two peaks, one at A+C/2, and one at A-C/2. answer: Perhaps a more interesting question is why doesn't just touching two solid metal blocks together weld them together? Why do we need to melt the metals to make them stick to each other? And the answer is that it does happen, just not usually to a degree that would be noticeable in everyday life. But under suitable conditions, such as in the vacuum of space, cold welding can and does in fact happen. But why, and why doesn't it occur normally on Earth? Well, the short answer is that most metallic surfaces on Earth are too rough and too dirty to stick together like that unless they're melted. For a more detailed answer, we need go a little bit into atomic theory. Basically, metals are made of many metal atoms. In solid and liquid states, these atoms stick to each other through metallic bonding , where the outer electrons of the atoms become delocalized and spread out across many atoms, bonding them together. (By the way, these delocalized electrons are also the reason why metals conduct electricity so well: not being tightly bound to individual atoms, these electrons can more easily move around and transport electric charge. And yes, I'm glossing over a lot of detail here. Follow the Wikipedia links if you want to dive deeper.) In a solid metal, the bonding is strong enough to pull the atoms together into a tightly packed crystal lattice (or several; most metals are polycrystalline ) and lock them in place there, making the metal rigid and able to hold its shape. Now, if you push two solid metallic surfaces close enough together, then there's in principle nothing stopping the delocalized electrons from jumping across the gap and bonding the atoms on both sides together into one solid piece of metal. And indeed, if the surfaces are very clean (down to the atomic level) and very flat (again to the atomic level, far below what even normal microscopes can see) or pushed together very strongly, so that there's absolutely no gap and no layer of other atoms in between them, then this will happen and the surfaces will effectively become welded together. However, it's very hard to make this happen under normal everyday conditions, because most metal surfaces — even those that look perfectly flat and clean to the naked eye, or even under a microscope — will have enough sub-microscopic irregularities and impurities to prevent it. If nothing else, just about any clean metal surface exposed to atmospheric oxygen almost instantly reacts with it, acquiring a very thin oxide coating that's enough to keep it from fully merging with another metal surface on contact. ( Optical contact bonding between very clean and flat metal surfaces, such as wrung gauge blocks , can and does still happen even in the presence of air. But such bonds are still much weaker than true welds, with the impurities and the imperfect contact between the surfaces creating enough weaknesses to allow the surfaces to be pulled apart again.) If the temperature of the metal is increased, however, the atoms making up its crystal lattice start moving around more and more, until eventually the metal melts into a liquid. In liquid metal, the atoms are still held together by metallic bonding, but they can move around much more freely and aren't stuck in a rigid crystal lattice. This has several effects that make it much easier for adjacent metals to merge together when molten: As the liquid metal flows, it can fill in any tiny gaps that may have existed between the surfaces in the solid state. As a liquid, the metal can also dissolve any impurities between the surfaces that may have prevented them from merging. Even any impurities that don't fully dissolve will tend to easily break apart into small fragments and mix with the molten metal once they no longer have a solid surface to attach to. Finally, in the molten state, the atoms from the two metals can even diffuse and blend together into one (more or less) uniform liquid. As a result, when the molten metal later cools down and solidifies again, the atoms will gradually settle into a new crystal lattice (or, again, usually several) that extends across the former gap between the original metal surfaces, welding them together and effectively making them part of the same continuous solid object.

answer: According to Airy wave theory the velocity potential for a monochromatic gravity wave with wavenumber $k$ and angular frequency $\omega$ is $$ \Phi = \frac{\omega}{k} a \frac{\cosh(k(z+h))}{\sinh (kh)} \sin (kx - \omega t) $$ where $h$ is the depth of the water. In the limit $h \to \infty$ (very deep water) this reduces to $$ \Phi \approx \frac{\omega}{k} a e^{-kz} \sin (kz - \omega t) $$ From this we see that $\Phi$ decreases exponentially with depth: $$ \Phi \propto e^{-kz} = e^{-2 \pi z/\lambda} $$ where $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the waves. The velocity potential is related to the water velocity $\vec{u}$ by $\vec{u} = \nabla \Phi$ , so the water velocities will decrease exponentially with depth at the same rate: for every wavelength you descend, the flow velocities decrease by a factor of $e^{-2 \pi} \approx 0.002$ . Thus, in practice, the water velocities will be practically zero once one descends more than a few wavelengths below the surface.

answer: Paper is much harder than cloth to transform non-isometrically due to its rigidity. Paper (at the force scales we can consider in this experiment, which I just did to help regain some intuition on the matter) is rigid in its own plane. That is, you can't compress or extend it very far compared to its own length on any axis parallel to the surface of the paper. If you try, you will eventually be made to put enough force in to tear the paper. It will happily break before it bends in this way. So, you can enforce things like conservation of curvature, which is honestly quite interesting to see in practice. Gauss's Theorema Egregium as it is otherwise called dictates that a local isometry does not affect the curvature of a surface; you can do any isometry you want and the curvature doesn't change (this includes deforming the paper through use of force or gravity, although sufficient force will of course break things down as the surface topology changes). Hence conservation of curvature, hence the paper has a distinct long axis along which it will not be made to bend without folding it. (Bending the paper along one axis like that is an isometry.) The trick is that the curvature is only invariant under isometries, not arbitrary transformations . Specifically, given metric spaces $A$ and $B$ with metrics $d_A(a_1,a_2):A\times A\to \mathbb{R}_+$ and $d_B(b_1, b_2):B\times B\to\mathbb{R}_+$ , an isometry is a map $f(a):A\to B$ such that $d_A(X, Y)=d_B(f(X), f(Y))$ for any $\{X, Y\}\subset A$ . That is, any set of points in $A$ must have the same distance between them as their corresponding points in $B$ . But real surfaces can be trivially made to disobey this rule. Consider the case where you "stretch" the surface along the $x$ -axis by 10%, so that $f(X)=(1.1X_x,X_y)$ , and the metrics on the initial paper and the final paper are both the ordinary Euclidean $d_A(X,Y)=d_B(X,Y)=\sqrt{(X_x-Y_x)^2+(X_y-Y_y)^2}$ . Obviously the isometry condition fails: picking points $X=(0,0)$ and $Y=(1,0)$ on the original surface, which are separated by distance $d_A(X,Y)=1$ , we see trivially that they correspond to $X'=(0,0)$ and $Y'=(1.1,0)$ which are separated by distance $d_B(X',Y')=1.1$ ; the transformation is non-isometric, and we have no reason to expect Gauss's remarkable theorem's conclusions to work here. To illustrate the difference without directly invoking differential geometry we can look at two examples: This is an example from Wikipedia of a shape undergoing an isometry. Note that the grid in both cases has preserved its spacing at every point: every square, if cut out and flattened a little bit, would be the same size between the two shapes. But of course there are plenty of transformations you can imagine --- almost definitionally all of which involve shortening or lengthening or shearing the squares about some in-plane axis --- which would not preserve this property across the transformation. Any such transformation is non-isometric. But the "stretching" that we would do in order to produce such a non-isometric transformation is of course very difficult to do in practice with paper. Paper is rather rigid on its two parallel axes, actually, and as we previously established it would quickly break before ever producing a meaningful deformation. A cloth is much more pliable than a piece of paper. It's not one sheet of cellulose, it's many threads woven together, so you can extend or compress it in-plane by substantial amounts without breaking it --- thereby producing a non-isometric transformation of the surface, allowing the Gaussian curvature to not be conserved because the theorem doing the conserving does not apply in this case.

answer: I'm a postdoc doing research in hep-th at a top institution. Everyone around me is feeding questions into LLMs. I've yet to see one produce an interesting answer. Perhaps part of the problem is that there are not many interesting open questions in hep-th, other than the two or three usual suspects e.g. come up with a testable theory of quantum gravity. In math you have concrete, precise questions, such as prove this or that theorem, or come up with a counterexample. In hep-th, the interesting questions are just too vague and open-ended, and require simultaneous input from multiple disciplines (experiments, pheno, various areas of cutting edge math, etc.). This seems too undetermined and loose for current LLMs. Note: by interesting I mean that ~10 or more people care. It's hard to think of a single interesting open question in hep-th whose answer could make the news. If someone manages to coax an LLM into computing, say, the seventh loop order of the Maldacena-Wilson loop in super Yang-Mills, would anyone care, other than the people that computed the sixth order by hand 20 years ago? So, to answer your question "Is AI affecting Physics as it is affecting Mathematics?": as far as I can tell, the answer is no. At the individual level, yes, nobody is doing algebra by hand anymore (much like when mathematica came out ~30 years ago). At the level of theoretical physics as a discipline, papers are basically the same, they just come out faster (and quality is going down, or rather, the signal-to-noise ratio has deteriorated substantially this past year). An example to illustrate this is perhaps the fact that openAI is paying Xi Yin to use their models, and he is using those resources to write a QFT textbook instead of trying to solve a novel problem. There is no physics version of the millennium problems. (Another half-example: a few months ago, people got mildly excited about a claim that chatGPT solved a problem in the field of scattering amplitudes . From what I can tell, most of the excitement came from the fact that one of the authors is very famous. answer: The Global Positioning System is, at its heart, a constellation of satellites which report precise times and locations. These enable any receiver to triangulate the receiver's location by comparing the propagation delays among several signals. Operating the GPS network requires general relativity, not just special relativity, because the local curvature of spacetime (which gives the local strength of the gravitational field) influences the rate at which identical clocks run. Earth's gravitational field strength decreases with altitude, so clocks in orbit run at different speeds compared to clocks on the ground, and clocks in different orbits will run at different speeds compared to one another. This general-relativistic effect is in addition to special-relativistic effects on clock rates due to the speeds of orbiting spacecraft compared to stationary observers on the ground. Smaller relativistic corrections must be applied by the receivers on the ground; see this excellent parallel answer . My favorite demonstration of general relativity's altitude-related time dilation is a classic (2005) kitchen-physics experiment from Tom Van Baak, a physicist whose kitchen happened to include a collection of atomic clocks. Van Baak took his kids and some of his atomic clocks camping on a mountaintop, where the weekend lasted 22 nanoseconds longer than it did for the atomic clocks which stayed home at sea level. He called it "the best 22 nanoseconds I've ever spent with my children." One story about GPS, which may or may not be true, is that there was debate among the design engineers about whether the general relativistic corrections were actually necessary. The first generation of satellites were therefore launched with the ability to run the onboard atomic clocks with or without the GR correction. Without the GR correction, the system didn't work at all. You can kind of see this from the Van Baak result. The speed of light is about one foot per nanosecond, so the error introduced by ignoring general relativity is about twenty feet per weekend per mountaintop. The altitude of a GPS satellite is many mountaintops, and GPS has been running for many, many weekends, and yet a precision of tens of feet is still quite achievable.
